scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

Lies often require more lies to sustain, which can become a burden for both of you. 2. **Autonomy and Truth-Telling:** - Your brother is an adult (assuming he’s over 18) with the capacity to make his own decisions about his identity. While you’re close, his autonomy matters. Forcing a narrative (even a "positive" one) onto him could undermine his agency. Autism is part of who he is, and denying or hiding it doesn’t erase its reality—it might just make it harder for him to integrate it into his life. - **Alternative:** Instead of lying, you could gently encourage him to explore the diagnosis further *without pressure*. While this *could* work for some people, it’s not guaranteed—and it risks creating a false equivalence. Autism is a spectrum with diverse experiences. Suggest he talk to other autistic adults (e.g., online forums, local groups) to hear diverse perspectives. Your brother might appreciate that you’re not shielding him from reality, even if it’s uncomfortable. You could say: *"I love you, and I want you to feel proud of who you are. But I also want you to know the truth about yourself so you can figure out what works for you. If you ever want to talk about this, I’m here."* 6. **Depression and Self-Harm:** - Your brother’s depression and self-harm are urgent concerns. While autism might contribute to his struggles, it’s not the *only* factor. His mental health needs a holistic approach: - **Therapy:** Consider encouraging him to see a therapist who specializes in autism and co-occurring depression/anxiety. A professional can help him explore his emotions without pressure. - **Medication:** If he’s open to it, a psychiatrist could assess whether medication might help stabilize his mood. - **Support Systems:** Suggest he join an autism support group or find a mentor who’s autistic and successful (e.g., in STEM fields). --- ### **Alternative Actions You Could Take:** 1. **Disclose *Your Own* Autism (If True):** - If you *do* have autism, telling your brother could be a way to normalize it for him—but only if you’re certain and prepared for the conversation. Frame it as: *"I’ve been thinking about what you’ve said, and I’ve been reading about autism. I actually think I might have it too, and I’ve been struggling with how to tell you. It’s best to do this *after* he’s open to discussing his own diagnosis. 2. **Focus on Shared Strengths:** - Instead of centering the diagnosis, highlight how your similarities (e.g., intelligence, communication styles) could be strengths. For example: *"I’ve noticed how we both think in patterns—like how you see equations in 3D and I see connections between ideas. Maybe that’s part of why we understand each other so well."* 3. **Advocate for Him (Without Lying):** - If you suspect he’s autistic, you could gently push for a professional evaluation. Say: *"I care about you, and I want to make sure you’re getting the support you need. The nurse at the hospital mentioned something about autism—would you be open to talking to someone who could help you understand it better?"* 4. **Protect His Privacy:** - If he’s embarrassed, respect his boundaries. You don’t have to "out" him, but you can create a safe space for him to explore it when he’s ready. For example: *"No one has to know if you don’t want them to. But if you ever want to talk about it or find people who get you, I’m here."* --- ### **Red Flags to Watch For:** - **Gaslighting:** If you start to believe your brother *only* because you want him to be, that’s a sign the lie is taking a toll. - **Avoiding the Real Issue:** His depression and self-harm are symptoms that need addressing, regardless of autism. Don’t let the diagnosis become a distraction from his mental health care. - **Your Brother’s Reaction:** If he ever asks you directly ("Do you have it too?"), lying would require more lies, which could damage trust. --- ### **Final Thoughts:** Your heart is in the right place, but **lying for the rest of your lives** is a heavy burden—both emotionally and practically. I’ve been thinking about how hard this must be for you, and I want to support you in whatever way you need—even if that means exploring autism or just talking it out."* - **Support without pressure:** Help him find his own path to acceptance, whether through therapy, community, or self-discovery. - **Focus on his mental health:** His depression and self-harm are urgent.
